about.title: The Internet and AI: Fast Copying, New Learners
about.length_note: About 45 minutes: 52 short beats and 15 questions. It covers six ideas, so you can pause after any section. If you need two sittings, stop after the source-checking section and finish with AI. I read the sources as search excerpts on 2026-11-03, not as full pages, so a person should check the full pages before publishing. I did not research wider world events, so the frame_of_reference list only holds computing and web events that the sources support. The class-wide history-of-everything timeline should supply the rest.

say.text: Welcome to class seven. Last time, printing and schools copied knowledge at scale. Today we look at two newer tools: the internet, and AI.

show.text: The Internet and AI: Fast Copying, New Learners

say.text: Six ideas, one at a time. Take your time, and pause whenever you like.

show.text:
1. Computers and the web
2. Checking a source
3. What AI is
4. AI and learning
5. Can AI improve itself? Fact or guess
6. Who gets to join in

say.text: Remember the ratchet from class one: each generation keeps what works and builds on it. Faster copying means the ratchet can turn faster.
First, the machines. In 1975 came a hobby kit, the Altair 8800. In 1977, the Apple II. In 1981, the IBM PC.

show.text:
1975: Altair 8800 kit
1977: Apple II
1981: IBM PC

say.text: A personal computer is one a single person can use. Apple gave away thousands of Apple IIs to schools, so many young people met a computer for the first time.
The IBM PC was widely copied by other makers, and a huge world of software grew around it. Copying a design spread the machine.

show.text: An early IBM PC: a beige box, a keyboard, and a screen showing plain text.

ask.q: Which order is right, earliest first?
wrong: IBM PC (1981), Altair 8800 (1975), Apple II (1977)
Apple II (1977), IBM PC (1981), Altair 8800 (1975)
Apple II (1977), Altair 8800 (1975), IBM PC (1981)
ask.why: The Altair kit came in 1975, the Apple II began shipping in 1977, and IBM announced its PC in 1981.

say.text: Now two words that get mixed up. The internet is the network joining computers. The web is linked pages you move through by clicking.

show.text: The internet: the network that carries information || The web: linked pages (hypertext) you click through

say.text: Tim Berners-Lee, a scientist at CERN, wrote the first proposal for the web in March 1989.

show.text: The first web page: plain text and links about the web project itself.

say.text: By the end of 1990 the first web server and browser were running at CERN. The software was released in 1991.

show.text:
Mar 1989: first proposal
12 Nov 1990: formal proposal with Robert Cailliau
End of 1990: first server and browser running
1991: software released
Dec 1991: first US web server (SLAC)
Late 1993: over 500 known web servers
1994: the 'Year of the Web'

say.text: In late 1993 the web was only about one percent of internet traffic. It seemed a lot back then.

ask.q: Where did the first US web server come online, in December 1991?
ask.right: At a particle physics laboratory (SLAC, in California)
wrong: At a newspaper office
At a high school
At a public library
ask.why: Early web servers were in physics laboratories. The first in the US was at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center.

say.text: Why was the web built? To let physicists share computer-stored information, not just at their lab, but around the world.

ask.q: What was the web first designed to help with?
ask.right: Physicists sharing information around the world
wrong: Selling products online
Streaming films
Playing computer games
ask.why: Berners-Lee's idea was a single information network so CERN physicists could share what was stored on computers.

say.text: Notice the pattern. Speech, writing, printing, and now the web: each one helps knowledge travel further.
Two more gifts. Search helps you find one page among millions. And sharing the tools lets others build on them.
Berners-Lee released the web software in 1991. CERN soon offered a much simpler browser that could run on any system.
Now the problem. Misinformation is false or misleading information. On the web anyone can publish, and a false claim can be copied as fast as a true one.
Stanford researchers watched how people check websites. Fact-checkers often clicked away from an unfamiliar site to see what others said about it. This is called lateral reading.
Here is a simple method with four moves, called SIFT. It was created by Mike Caulfield.
S is for Stop. Pause before you believe it or share it. Ask yourself: do I know this source?
I is for Investigate the source. Who wrote it? What do they want? Do they know this subject?
F is for Find better coverage. See whether other trusted sources agree, or disagree.
T is for Trace. If a story quotes an expert or a study, find the original. Retellings can leave out important context.

ask.q: An article quotes a study. What does 'Trace' ask you to do?
ask.right: Find the original study and read what it actually says
wrong: Count how many times the article was shared
Trust it because it sounds scientific
Check the colour and design of the website
ask.why: Following a claim back to its original source helps you spot facts or context that were left out.

say.text: Example. A site you have never heard of makes a shocking claim. Don't scroll through it. Open a new tab and look up the site's name.

show.text: A browser with two tabs: the shocking page on the left tab, a search about the site's name on the right tab.

ask.q: Unfamiliar site, shocking claim. What is the best first move?
ask.right: Open a new tab and see what trusted sources say about the site
wrong: Read only the site's own 'About us' page and stop there
Share it quickly so friends can judge
Scroll through the whole page very carefully
ask.why: Lateral reading means leaving the page to check who is behind it. The site's own About page is not enough.

say.text: Now AI. Many chat tools run on a large language model. It is a computer program trained on huge amounts of text.
Training means practising prediction: guess the next word in a piece of text, again and again, across a huge pile of writing.
People wrote that text. So the model is built from the pile of human knowledge that the ratchet left behind. Some systems are trained on other kinds of data besides text.

show.text: Made by people: the writing the model learns from || Made by the model: new text built from patterns it learned

say.text: The Transformer design that powers these tools was published in 2017. ChatGPT appeared in November 2022.

show.text:
2017: the Transformer paper ('Attention Is All You Need')
Nov 2022: ChatGPT

ask.q: What does a language model learn from?
ask.right: Huge amounts of human-written text, practising next-word prediction
wrong: One expert who checks every answer
Only the questions you type today
A hand-written list of every true fact
ask.why: Pretraining means predicting the next word across a huge amount of text.

say.text: So an AI is a new kind of learner. It takes in a vast pile of writing and copies its patterns, fast and wide.
But in pretraining it sees only examples of fluent language. Nobody marks each sentence as true or false.

show.text: Fluent is not the same as true

say.text: When an AI gives a confident answer that isn't true, that is called a hallucination.
Why does it happen? OpenAI researchers argue that training and testing reward guessing over saying 'I'm not sure', like a student guessing on a hard exam.
Rare facts are the risky ones. In the paper's example, if a fifth of birthday facts appear only once in training, expect errors on at least a fifth of them.

ask.right: A confident answer from an AI that is not true
wrong: A picture the AI draws
A message saying the AI is switched off
A correct answer found by searching the web
ask.why: Hallucination means a model confidently giving an answer that isn't true.

say.text: Now a real test. Nearly a thousand high school maths students used AI tutors in a field experiment, at one high school in Turkey.
One tutor worked like a plain chatbot. The other had prompts built to protect learning. Access to AI improved performance on practice.

show.text: Plain chatbot tutor || Tutor with learning safeguards

say.text: But without guardrails, AI help could substantially inhibit learning. The safeguards largely reduced that harm, though the study saw no clear gain.

ask.q: What did the study find about unguarded AI help?
ask.right: It raised practice performance but could weaken learning
wrong: It made learning much stronger
It had no effect at all
It only helped students who were already top of the class
ask.why: The researchers found access to AI can improve performance while substantially inhibiting learning without guardrails.

say.text: So how can you use AI well for learning? Try first yourself, ask for hints or explanations, and always check what it says.

show.text:
Try the problem first
Ask for hints and explanations
Check its answers (use SIFT)
Remember: AI is fallible

say.text: Big question next. Can AI help improve AI, and then improve itself again? Machines helping to design better versions of themselves is called recursive self-improvement.
People already do a human version of this: tools build better tools, and science improves its own methods. That was class six.
The idea is old. In the mid-1960s the mathematician I. J. Good wrote that a machine could design better machines. He called the result an 'intelligence explosion'.

show.text:
Mid-1960s: I. J. Good describes an 'intelligence explosion' (an idea)
2017: Transformer paper
Nov 2022: ChatGPT

say.text: Keep two things apart: what has happened, and what someone predicts. Here they are side by side.

show.text: Known now: AI is starting to help with AI work; humans are still in the loop || Only predicted: a runaway 'intelligence explosion'; dates like 2027

say.text: Known now: AI is starting to help build better AI, but humans are still in the loop. Leading labs still need human oversight for high-level decisions.

show.text: Known: humans still in the loop

ask.q: Which of these is a present fact, not a prediction?
ask.right: Humans still oversee high-level decisions in AI development
wrong: AI will certainly outthink all people by 2027
An uncontrollable intelligence explosion is already under way
Self-improving AI will definitely end humanity
ask.why: Reports describe models as still needing human oversight. The other statements are forecasts or claims about the future.

say.text: Now predictions. Some essays project superintelligence by 2027, or by the end of this decade. And some leading researchers call an intelligence explosion a credible risk.

ask.q: Which statement is a prediction about the future?
wrong: I. J. Good wrote about an intelligence explosion in the 1960s
ChatGPT appeared in November 2022
The Transformer paper was published in 2017
ask.why: The other three are dated records of things that already happened. The first one is a forecast that nobody can yet check.

say.text: Experts disagree. Skeptics say new ideas must be tested with huge amounts of computing, so smarter thinking alone could hit a limit.
Another paper argued the barriers are high, though it called this not a decisive argument. Others say the idea is partly hype.

ask.q: Why do some skeptics doubt a fast runaway loop?
ask.right: Testing ideas takes lots of computing and experiments, which can slow it down
wrong: Computers cannot do any research
Every expert agrees it is impossible
Humans have banned all AI research
ask.why: One paper argues that ideas must be tested in compute-heavy experiments, so a loop could fizzle.

say.text: The honest summary: the loop is an idea with early, partial signs. How fast or far it goes is not known.
Last section: who gets to take part? The ITU estimates 6 billion people were online in 2025, about three-quarters of the world. And 2.2 billion were not.
That is growth: from 60 percent online in 2020 to 74 percent in 2025.
But the gaps are big. 94 percent online in high-income countries, 23 percent in low-income ones. Cities are ahead of rural areas, and men slightly ahead of women.

show.text: Share of people online, 2025, by group

ask.q: Where do most people who are offline live?
ask.right: In low- and middle-income countries (96 percent of those offline)
wrong: In high-income countries
Mostly in big cities
Nobody can say
ask.why: ITU reports that 96 percent of people offline live in low- and middle-income countries.

say.text: Cost and quality matter too. ITU's head says today's divides come from speed, reliability, affordability and skills. 'Online' is not one thing.
Language is another gate. W3Techs finds English on about half of websites whose language is known. Spanish comes next at about six percent.

show.text: Share of websites by content language, October 2026

say.text: Measuring this is hard. One study argues English is nearer 20 to 30 percent of web content. Either way, W3Techs lists Hindi, Swahili and Tamil under 0.1 percent of sites.
A reasoning step, not a measured result here: if AI learns from web text, languages with less text give it less to learn from.
Now disability. The web's stewards put access at the centre of the design.

show.text: Access by everyone regardless of disability is an essential aspect. (W3C)

say.text: The standard is called WCAG. It explains how to make web content usable for people with disabilities, including people who use screen readers or voice commands.
It helps others too, like someone with a broken arm, or someone in bright sunlight. The W3C started its accessibility work in 1997.

ask.right: International guidelines for making web content accessible to people with disabilities
wrong: A search engine
A type of AI model
A programming language for building apps
ask.why: WCAG is developed within the W3C Web Accessibility Initiative to explain how to make web content accessible.

say.text: Let us put the dates in one place, for the history-of-everything timeline.

show.text:
1975: Altair 8800 kit
1977: Apple II
1981: IBM PC
Mar 1989: first web proposal
End of 1990: first web server and browser running
Dec 1991: first US web server
1997: W3C starts its Web Accessibility Initiative
2017: Transformer paper
Nov 2022: ChatGPT

say.text: To remember: the web shares fast, so check sources with SIFT. AI learns from human text and can be wrong. Self-improving AI is an idea, not a settled fact. And access is uneven.

show.text:
The web shares fast: check with SIFT
AI learns from human text and can be wrong
Self-improving AI: idea, early signs, big disagreement
Access is uneven: place, cost, language, disability

say.text: Next class: how knowledge gets lost. Faster copying helps, but copies can vanish too.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: In computing, the Altair 8800 kit appeared on a hobby magazine cover in January. Its buzz pushed Bill Gates and Paul Allen to start a software company for it.
Apple began shipping the Apple II in June, and Apple gave away thousands of them to schools.
IBM announced its PC. It was widely cloned, and a large software ecosystem grew around it.
The web was proposed in March 1989, ran on a first server by the end of 1990, and reached its first US server in December 1991. That same year the European Commission approved its first web project.
The W3C launched its Web Accessibility Initiative.
The Transformer design was published in 2017, and ChatGPT appeared in November 2022.

other_side.claim: AI may soon improve itself in a runaway 'intelligence explosion'.
other_side.other_view: Some experts take this seriously. In one study of 25 AI experts, all but two entertained the idea. Some leading researchers call it a credible risk. Skeptics argue that testing ideas needs huge computing power, that barriers to self-improvement are high, and that the term is partly hype. Current systems still need human oversight.

other_side.claim: English makes up about half of the web.
other_side.other_view: W3Techs reports English on about half of sites with a known language. One research paper argues that English content is nearer 20 to 30 percent when multilingual sites are counted properly. Methods differ, and the two figures measure different things.

In a school experiment, unguarded AI raised practice performance but could substantially inhibit learning. Safeguards largely removed the harm, but no clear gain in learning was seen. It was one school and one subject, so more evidence is needed.

other_side.claim: AI hallucinations can never be avoided.
other_side.other_view: OpenAI's researchers argue hallucinations are not inevitable, because models can decline to answer when unsure. They say current training and scoring rewards guessing, and that this could be changed. Hallucinations persist in current models.

other_side.claim: The web opened knowledge to everyone.
other_side.other_view: About 2.2 billion people were still offline in 2025, mostly in low- and middle-income countries. Cost, speed, skills, language and disability can still be barriers for people who are online.
